title: The tower clock
bodyMd:
Every Thursday at seven Nando Baresi climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the clock tower, and every Thursday he stopped on the sixtieth to rest, though he would have denied that he needed to. Elena Moretti, who had been sent by the town council to learn the mechanism before it was replaced by a radio-controlled unit, waited two steps below him with the oilcan and pretended not to notice.

The machine room smelled of brass and pigeons. Nando raised the weights hand over hand, as he had done for forty-one years, and let the pendulum swing a while before he spoke.

‘It runs four minutes fast,’ he said. ‘The council's letter calls that a fault.’

‘Isn't it?’ Elena asked.

‘It was set that way in 1962. The station clock had been moved across the square, and people in the piazza kept missing the 8.10 to Alessandria because the tower said one time and the platform another. The keeper of the day put the tower ahead, so that anyone who trusted it would arrive early.’ He wiped his hands on a cloth that had once been white. ‘Nobody wrote it down. It was simply something one told the next keeper.’

Elena looked at the dial from behind, its numerals reversed and grey with dust. She had brought a laptop, and it lay unopened in her bag. On the way up she had rehearsed how to explain, kindly, that the new unit would be accurate to a second a year.

‘The new unit will keep perfect time,’ she said at last.

‘I am sure it will.’ He sounded like a man agreeing about the weather. He did not turn round. ‘Come and see where the oil goes.’

For an hour he showed her the pawls and the escapement, and she oiled what he pointed to. She did not mention the laptop again. But when they came down as far as the sixtieth step, and Nando stopped there as usual to examine a crack in the plaster that neither of them believed was of interest, she took the laptop out, balanced it on her knee and typed a single line into the file headed Notes for the installer: Set the tower four minutes ahead. Nando, standing a few steps below her with his back turned, could not possibly have seen the screen; but he nodded as though he had read it.
accessibilityText: A short narrative of about 400 words. Every Thursday Nando Baresi, keeper of a town clock tower, climbs its hundred and twelve steps and stops on the sixtieth to rest, while Elena Moretti, sent by the council to learn the mechanism before a radio-controlled unit replaces it, waits below with the oilcan and pretends not to notice. In the machine room Nando says the clock runs four minutes fast and that the council's letter calls this a fault. He explains that it was set that way in 1962: the station clock had been moved and people in the piazza kept missing the 8.10 to Alessandria, so the keeper of the day put the tower ahead so that anyone who trusted it would arrive early. Nobody wrote this down; it was something one told the next keeper. Elena, who had rehearsed how to explain kindly that the new unit will be accurate to a second a year, says only that it will keep perfect time, and Nando agrees without turning round and shows her where the oil goes. On the way down, when Nando stops again on the sixtieth step, Elena types a single line into her notes for the installer: set the tower four minutes ahead. Nando, standing below with his back turned, cannot have seen the screen, but he nods as though he had read it.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The tower, the town, the two characters, the council and the 1962 episode are invented. The 8.10 to Alessandria is an invented timetable detail, not a reference to a real service. No published text was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed, and no author is quoted.
